heading.what: Headings are titles that label each part of a page, from the main title (h1) down to small sub-sections (h6). They give a page an outline that people and software can scan.
uses: Breaking long articles, documentation and reports into scannable sections.
Letting screen-reader users jump between sections.
Showing the main topic of a page in one h1.
avoid: Making text bigger or bold only for looks: use a style, not a heading level.
Labelling single items like buttons or form fields: use the proper label element.
practices: Use one h1 per page.
Go down one level at a time and never skip levels.
Choose the level for the outline, then adjust the look with styling.
Keep headings short and specific.

page-title.what: The page title is the main heading of a page. It tells people which page or item they are on.
uses: Naming the page at the top of an application screen.
Naming the record on a detail page.
Giving every page one clear focal point.
avoid: Putting the site name in every title: use a logo or header for the brand.
Long explanations: use a subtitle or help text.
practices: Name the thing, such as 'Orders', not the action.
Put the distinguishing word first.
Make it the page's single h1.
Match the browser tab title.

page-subtitle.what: A page subtitle is one short sentence under the page title. It explains what the page is for or adds one key fact.
uses: Clarifying a page whose title alone is vague.
Showing scope, such as a date range or filter.
Giving first-time visitors a hint of what to do.
avoid: Restating the title in other words: leave it out.
Long instructions: put help text next to the field that needs it.
practices: Keep it to one short sentence.
Make it add something the title does not.
Use a quieter colour than the title.
Keep lines a readable length.

section-title.what: A section title heads a group of related content on a page, such as a set of panels or part of a long form.
uses: Splitting a long page into a few named parts.
Grouping related fields in a long form.
Helping people scan to the part they need.
avoid: Titling a section that holds only one titled panel: the panel title is enough.
Naming the whole page: use the page title.
practices: Use words people would look for, not 'Other' or 'Misc'.
Keep the heading level in order.
Leave more space above than below.
Keep titles to a few words.

panel-title.what: A panel title is the heading of a boxed block of content, such as a card, table or chart. It names what that block shows.
uses: Naming a chart, table or summary card.
Heading a settings group in a box.
Letting people find a block by scanning.
avoid: Naming a whole page section: use a section title.
Styling that looks like a link or label, such as colour or all capitals.
practices: Describe the content in a few words.
Pick the heading level that fits the page outline.
Add a short muted description only if needed.
Keep style the same on every panel.

alert-title.what: An alert title is the bold first line of a message box. It states plainly what happened so the reader can decide quickly.
uses: Naming the result in a success or error message.
Heading a warning or notice with a longer body.
Giving screen-reader users the key fact first.
avoid: One-line messages: skip the title and write one clear sentence.
Vague titles like 'Error' or 'Oops': state the problem.
practices: State the fact, such as 'Report sent'.
Keep it to a few words.
Skip 'Error:' prefixes and exclamation marks.
Follow it with what to do next.

paragraph.what: A paragraph is a block of running text. It carries explanations and descriptions, and its size and line length set how easy a page is to read.
uses: Explaining a feature or a result.
Writing the body of a dialog or message.
Introducing a section before lists or tables.
avoid: Long blocks of dense text: split them or use a list.
Content that is really a list of steps: use a numbered list.
practices: Put the main point first.
Keep one idea in each paragraph.
Keep lines around 60 to 75 characters.
Use short sentences.

text-link.what: A text link is clickable text that takes the reader to another page, file or place on the same page.
uses: Pointing to related pages from within a sentence.
Linking to outside sources or documentation.
Jumping to a section on the same page.
avoid: Actions that change data, such as save or delete: use a button.
Vague text like 'click here': say where the link goes.
practices: Make link text meaningful on its own.
Underline links so colour is not the only cue.
Show a clear focus outline.
Say when a link opens another site.

muted-text.what: Muted text is secondary text shown in a softer colour so the main content stands out. It must still be easy to read.
uses: Showing descriptions under titles.
Showing meta details such as counts or dates.
Showing empty values like 'Not set'.
avoid: Text people must read to finish a task: use normal colour.
Showing that something is disabled: use a real disabled state.
practices: Keep enough contrast: at least 4.5 to 1 against the background.
Do not rely on pale grey.
Use it only for secondary information.

small-text.what: Small text is a smaller type size for supporting information such as help, captions and timestamps.
uses: Writing help text under a field.
Showing captions, timestamps or footnotes.
Adding meta details next to a title.
avoid: Body copy or anything essential to read in full: use normal text size.
Legal or critical warnings: keep them at normal size.
practices: Do not go below about 14px.
Keep contrast high.
Keep it short.
Pair it with a quieter colour for meta details.

tabular-number.what: Tabular numbers use digits of equal width, so figures line up in columns and do not shift when values change.
uses: Showing prices and totals in tables.
Showing live counters and timers.
Showing times, durations and percentages.
avoid: Running text and headings: normal digits read more naturally there.
Codes with letters and digits, such as IDs: use a monospace code style.
practices: Right-align numbers in columns.
Add thousand separators and units.
Use the same decimal places in a column.
Use it for values that update.

kbd.what: A keyboard key element shows a key or key combination in a key-like shape, so readers can tell it from the surrounding sentence.
uses: Documenting shortcuts in help text.
Showing shortcuts next to menu items.
Writing instructions that name specific keys.
avoid: Showing code or commands: use a code style.
Making a shortcut the only way to do something: always offer a visible option.
practices: Use one element per key.
Write key names as printed, such as Ctrl or Esc.
Join combinations with a plus sign.
Consider Mac and Windows differences.

stat-label.what: A stat label is the short name of a measured value, shown with the number so readers know what it means.
uses: Naming a number on a dashboard tile.
Labelling a figure in a summary row.
Telling apart several similar numbers.
avoid: Long explanations: use a tooltip or help text.
Labels that repeat the whole tile title.
practices: Name the measure and its scope, such as 'Visitors today'.
Keep it to a few words.
Place it consistently above or beside the value.
Use sentence case.

stat-value.what: A stat value is a large number that shows one key measurement. It is the main thing a summary tile is there to show.
uses: Showing key figures on a dashboard.
Opening a report with headline numbers.
Showing a live count.
avoid: Many figures in one tile: use a table or chart.
Numbers without context: add a label, unit or comparison.
practices: Show one main value per tile.
Include the unit, such as % or h.
Format with thousand separators.
Use equal-width digits.

delta.what: A delta shows how a value changed compared with an earlier period or a target, using an arrow, a signed number and a colour.
uses: Comparing today with yesterday on a KPI tile.
Showing growth or decline over a period.
Showing distance from a target.
avoid: Showing a total on its own: use a stat value.
Using red and green alone: add an arrow and a sign.
practices: Show direction with an arrow and sign, not colour alone.
Say what it is compared with.
Colour by good or bad, not up or down.
Use a true minus sign.

code-text.what: Code text shows short technical values in a monospace font, so they stand out from sentences and characters are easy to tell apart.
uses: Showing file names, paths and IDs.
Showing short commands or settings keys.
Showing values people may copy.
avoid: Many lines of code: use a code block.
Emphasising ordinary words: use bold or italic.
practices: Use it only for literal values.
Let long values wrap.
Offer a copy button for values people copy.
Keep contrast high.

card-kicker.what: A card kicker is a short label above a card title that names the card's category, such as 'Video' or 'Guide'.
uses: Telling types apart in a mixed list of cards.
Adding a category to news or article cards.
Helping people scan a grid.
avoid: Showing status such as 'Draft' or 'Failed': use a badge.
Long labels: keep kickers to one to three words.
practices: Use one to three words.
Use the same wording across cards.
Keep it quieter than the title.
Use capitals only for short labels.

card-title.what: A card title is the name of the item a card stands for. It is the first thing people read in a grid of cards.
uses: Naming a record, product or article card.
Giving a clickable card its link text.
Helping people choose between cards.
avoid: Decorative or vague titles: use the real name of the item.
Cutting off long names: let them wrap.
practices: Use the item's real name.
Keep the distinguishing words visible.
Use the same heading level on every card.
Make link text clear if the card is a link.

card-meta.what: Card meta is a line of small secondary facts under a card title, such as type, date or count.
uses: Showing dates, sizes or counts on a card.
Showing the source or author of an item.
Giving extra detail without crowding the title.
avoid: Key facts people need to decide: put them in the title or body.
Long lists of facts: link to a detail page.
practices: Show three facts at most.
Separate facts with a dot or space.
Use a quieter style than the title.
Keep the order the same on every card.

dialog-title.what: A dialog title is the heading of a pop-up window. It says in a few words what the person is being asked or told.
uses: Naming a confirmation, such as 'Delete this file?'.
Titling a form shown in a dialog.
Naming a side panel or drawer.
avoid: Vague titles like 'Warning' or 'Are you sure?': name the action and object.
Long text: put detail in the body.
practices: Ask the question or name the task.
Mention the object affected.
Repeat the verb on the main button.
Link the title to the dialog for screen readers.

empty-title.what: An empty-state title is the short heading shown when a list, table or search has nothing to display. It says plainly what is missing.
uses: Showing a new, empty list.
Showing a search or filter with no matches.
Showing a chart with no data yet.
avoid: Content that is still loading: show a loading state instead.
Errors: use an error message that says what went wrong.
practices: State what is missing in plain words.
Keep it calm and short.
Avoid blaming the person.
Pair it with a next step.

empty-text.what: Empty-state text is a short sentence under the empty-state title. It explains why nothing is shown and what to do next.
uses: Inviting people to create their first item.
Suggesting they clear filters after no results.
Explaining why data is not there yet.
avoid: Long help articles: link to documentation.
Jokes or blame in work tools: stay neutral and useful.
practices: Say what to do next.
Keep it to one or two sentences.
Offer the action as a button.
Fit the text to the cause, new or filtered.

generic-list.what: A list page shows many records of one kind, with a title, search or filters, sortable rows and paging. It is the most common screen in business applications.
uses: Browsing orders, customers or other records.
Finding and opening a record.
Adding a new record from the list.
avoid: Comparing a few items in depth: use a detail or comparison view.
Browsing visual items: a card grid may suit better.
practices: Show the total count.
Offer search and filters for long lists.
Add paging for long lists.
Show a helpful empty state and a no-results state.
Make rows open the record.

generic-detail.what: A detail page shows everything about one record as label and value pairs, with the actions that apply to it, such as edit or delete.
uses: Reading all fields of a record.
Starting an edit or a delete.
Checking a record before acting on it.
avoid: Editing fields: use a form page.
Browsing many records: use a list page.
practices: Put the record's name in the title.
Show label and value pairs in a steady order.
Keep actions in the same place on every record.
Show empty values clearly.

generic-form.what: A form page is a page whose main job is one form to create or edit a record, with save and cancel actions.
uses: Creating a new record.
Editing an existing record.
Collecting a few inputs on a page of their own.
avoid: Very short edits: edit in place or in a dialog.
Long, many-step processes: use a step-by-step flow.
practices: Use one column of fields.
Put clear labels above fields.
Show an error summary and inline errors.
Make Save the clear main action and add Cancel.

generic-confirm-delete.what: A delete confirmation page asks people to confirm before a record is removed. It says what will be lost, or why it cannot be deleted.
uses: Confirming permanent removal.
Explaining what else will be removed.
Explaining that related records block deletion.
avoid: Deletes that can be undone: allow undo instead of asking first.
Minor, low-cost actions: do not add confirmation.
practices: Name the record being deleted.
List what will be lost.
Label the button with the action, such as 'Delete order'.
Make Cancel easy to find.

generic-confirm-action.what: A confirm-action page asks for a second look before a consequential action that is not a delete, such as sending to everyone or disabling something.
uses: Sending a message to many people.
Disabling or archiving a site or account.
Starting a long or costly run.
avoid: Harmless, easily undone actions: just do them.
Deleting: use the delete confirmation.
practices: Ask a clear question.
List the consequences.
Name the button with the action's verb.
Use a danger style only when something is lost.

parent-base.what: A parent page is the shared frame for a record that owns other records. It keeps the record's title and tabs in place while the content changes.
uses: Showing a project with its tasks and files.
Showing a customer with orders and invoices.
Keeping people oriented across related pages.
avoid: Records with no related lists: use a single detail page.
Unrelated pages: use normal navigation.
practices: Keep the header and tabs identical on every tab.
Mark the current tab.
Give each tab its own address.
Show key figures above the tabs.

parent-detail.what: A parent overview tab shows the main facts about a record that owns other records, before its related lists.
uses: Showing the main details of a project, site or customer.
Starting point before related lists.
Adding summary panels.
avoid: Long related lists: put them on their own tabs.
Editing: use a form page.
practices: Make Overview the first tab.
Show label and value pairs.
Keep it short.
Link to the related lists.

parent-child-list.what: A child list tab shows the records that belong to a parent, such as the tasks of a project, with a count and an add action.
uses: Listing items owned by one parent.
Adding a new item to that parent.
Showing how many related items exist.
avoid: Listing records from many parents: use a normal list page.
Single related item: show it on the overview.
practices: Name the parent in the add button.
Show a count.
Name the parent in the empty state.
Add paging for long lists.

parent-child-detail.what: A child detail page shows one record that belongs to a parent, while keeping the parent's header and a way back to the list.
uses: Reading a single task, invoice or video of a parent.
Starting an edit or a delete.
Moving back to the parent's list.
avoid: Records that stand alone: use a normal detail page.
Editing: use a form page.
practices: Provide a back link to the list.
Keep the parent's header visible.
Place edit and delete beside the title.
Use a steady field order.

parent-child-form.what: A child form page creates or edits a record that belongs to a parent, with a heading that names the parent.
uses: Adding a new item to a parent.
Editing an item of a parent.
Keeping context while entering data.
avoid: Items that belong to no parent: use a normal form page.
Tiny edits: edit in place.
practices: Name the parent in the heading.
Do not ask people to choose the parent again.
Use one column of fields.
Add Cancel back to the list.

parent-child-confirm.what: A child confirm page asks people to confirm removing a record from its parent, or explains why it cannot be removed.
uses: Confirming removal of an item from a parent.
Explaining what else will go with it.
Explaining why removal is blocked.
avoid: Actions that can be undone: offer undo instead.
Deleting a whole parent: use a delete confirmation.
practices: Name both the item and the parent.
List the consequences.
Name the button with the verb.
Give a way to cancel.

button-group.what: A button group is a set of related buttons placed together. Joined buttons act on the same thing, and spaced ones are separate actions.
uses: Offering alternatives on one object, such as zoom in and out.
Grouping related actions like Export and Print.
Keeping toolbars tidy.
avoid: Choosing one mode among several: use a segmented control or toggle buttons.
Many actions: use a menu.
practices: Keep a consistent style in a group.
Label the group for screen readers.
Keep destructive actions apart.
Keep a group to a few buttons.

dropdown-menu.what: A dropdown menu is a button that opens a list of actions. It hides less common actions to keep the screen simple.
uses: Grouping secondary actions on a record.
Account or user menus.
An 'Add' button with several kinds.
avoid: Choosing a value for a field: use a select.
The main action: show it as a visible button.
practices: Make the menu work with the keyboard.
Put destructive items last.
Use short verb labels.
Close on Escape and return focus.

dropdown-item.what: A dropdown item is one action in a menu, shown as a row with a label and often an icon, description or shortcut.
uses: Listing actions in a menu.
Showing a shortcut next to an action.
Explaining why an action is unavailable.
avoid: Navigation between main sections: use navigation links.
Setting options: use a checkbox or radio menu item.
practices: Start labels with a verb.
Use icons the same way on every row.
Mark destructive items clearly.
Say why an item is disabled.

copy-button.what: A copy button copies a value to the clipboard in one click and confirms that it worked.
uses: Copying API keys, links or IDs.
Copying commands or addresses.
Avoiding typing mistakes with exact values.
avoid: Long documents: offer a download instead.
Secrets that must not be shown: do not display them.
practices: Show the value next to the button.
Confirm with 'Copied' and announce it to screen readers.
Give a fallback if the clipboard is blocked.
Keep the label clear.

record-actions.what: Record actions put the main action of a record in view and tuck the others into a 'More actions' menu.
uses: The header of a detail page.
A card with several actions.
Keeping a toolbar simple.
avoid: Records with one action: show only a button.
Many equal actions: consider a toolbar.
practices: Show one main action.
Name the record in the menu button's label.
Put destructive actions last.
Ask before destructive actions.

row-actions.what: Row actions are small buttons at the end of a table row that act on that row, with extra actions in a menu.
uses: Editing or viewing a row.
Opening a menu of more actions.
Acting on a row without leaving the table.
avoid: Actions for many rows at once: use bulk selection.
Hover-only actions: they fail on touch screens and keyboards.
practices: Show at most two actions.
Name the row in each button's label.
Keep actions always visible.
Use a quiet button style.

page-landmarks.what: Page landmarks are the main regions every page has, such as a skip link, the main content and navigation. They let assistive technology jump straight to the content.
uses: Letting keyboard users skip repeated navigation.
Helping screen-reader users move between regions.
Giving dialogs one place to open.
avoid: Dividing content for looks only: use plain containers.
Multiple main areas: use only one per page.
practices: Use one main region per page.
Make the skip link the first thing to tab to.
Label regions that appear more than once.
Use real landmark elements.

error-message.what: An error page tells people that something went wrong, such as a missing page or a server problem, in plain words and offers a way forward.
uses: Showing a page not found (404).
Showing no access (403) or server error (500).
Replacing a section that cannot load.
avoid: Mistakes in a form: show inline field errors.
Short-lived issues: show a banner or toast.
practices: Say what happened in plain words.
Offer a clear next step.
Do not blame the person.
Never show technical traces.

card-grid.what: A card grid arranges cards in equal columns that adjust to the screen width. It suits browsing a collection.
uses: Browsing products, people or media.
Showing records with an image.
Dashboards of equal items.
avoid: Comparing items field by field: use a table.
A single long list of text: use a list.
practices: Keep cards equal in size and layout.
Put content in the same order in each card.
Make the whole card clickable if it opens a record.
Keep spacing even.

loading-placeholder.what: A loading placeholder shows grey shapes in the form of the content while it loads. It keeps the layout stable and shows that something is coming.
uses: Loading a grid or feed.
Loading more items on scroll.
Loading content that takes over a second.
avoid: Very quick loads: show nothing extra.
Long processes with known progress: use a progress bar.
practices: Match the shape of the final content.
Mark the region as busy for screen readers.
Replace it all at once.
Avoid layout shifts.

no-results.what: A no-results state is what a list, table or search shows when there is nothing to display. It explains why and what to do next.
uses: A new list with no items yet.
A search or filter that matches nothing.
A feed that is empty.
avoid: Content that is still loading: show a loading state.
Errors: use an error message.
practices: Say whether it is empty or filtered.
Offer a clear next step.
Show the active filters and a Clear all action.
Keep the tone calm.
